newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Austria's Liebscher sees room for repo cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Austria's Liebscher sees room for repo cut.

text.p: Austrian central bank president Klaus Liebscher, kicking off a renewed round of interest rate speculation, said on Monday there was room for a downward move in the country's securities repurchase rate.
"There have been voices in Germany over the past few days saying the interest rate low has been reached -- I take note of that but I still see room in the repo rate," Liebscher told reporters.
The Austrian central bank cut its repo rate to three percent from 3.2 percent on September 2. It's discount rate was shaved to a historic low of 2.5 percent in April.
German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Friday economic growth was picking up and he saw no need for easier interest rates in the foreseeable future.

Austria, which joined the European exchange rate mechanism at the start of last year, closely follows the German central bank's monetary lead. Its currency, the schilling, has been pegged to the German mark since 1979.
Liebscher said the Austrian economy, benefiting from an upturn in Germany, showed strong signs of economic recovery.
"Economic recovery in western Europe is under way. The trough is behind us," he said. "We expect an uptick in foreign demand next year which should help improve exports."

However, Liebscher noted there was little room to expect an improvement in Austria's record current account deficit, estimated to remain at around two percent of gross domestic product because of a strong decline in tourism revenues.

The central bank chief added it was unlikely that all European Union member states would be able to join Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 and take part in the single currency, the euro.

"In the interest of the euro's stability the number of members joining in the first wave is crucial. I see those countries that are already viewed as the most economically stable as being in the first wave -- six, seven, or eight of them," he said. "I have no problem with such a small group."

Liebscher declined to say which countries would be able to meet the strict Maastricht criteria on inflation, debt and interest rates in time for EMU, but reiterated Austria would certainly be among them. "I am convinced that we can reach that goal," Liebscher said.
He warned against any watering down of the membership criteria to help some countries to make the mark.
"A watering down of the criteria is absolutely out of the question and so is a postponement," he said.
